sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** and **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job?** (one problem). Six phrases are both italic and underlined: "arrive before ten" (≈258–430, y≈178), "labelled with their ingredients" (≈419–734, y≈219), "three o'clock sharp," (≈517–712, y≈324), "collected by four" (≈180–350, y≈365), and "on the field / only" (≈843–960, y≈365 and ≈180–226, y≈406). On a screen, underlined text means a link, so the viewer reads these as six links. They may click them and get nothing, or they may wonder what they're missing. The underline adds nothing the italic doesn't already do, so its only effect is to mislead. On top of that, emphasising six phrases in five lines means none of them stands out. Underlined text being a link is the standard on screens (Nielsen, *10 Usability Heuristics*, no. 4: Consistency and standards). That the doubled styling does no job is common sense (the "every ornament does a job" sources are off the reading list). **Fix direction:** drop the underline so emphasis can't be mistaken for a link. Then cut the emphasis to what people have to act on (the times and the parking rule), or pull those out as a short list of times and rules. Convention, with a defect's consequence. **Weight: major**, because the emphasis is the piece's whole way of flagging what matters, and right now it reads as links and flags everything equally.
2. **Copy (no checklist line; welcome per critic.md).** "all tickets must be collected by four or the prizes go back in the box" (y≈324–365) can be read two ways: winners must collect their prizes by four, or organisers must collect the tickets by four. It's a deadline people will hold the organisers to, and someone who reads it the wrong way loses a prize. **Fix direction:** say who does what, e.g. "Winners must collect their prizes by four, or…". Defect. **Weight: minor** for this section. The director should judge it alongside the Text section.

**What's working.**
- One clear headline and two short paragraphs that cover arrival and cakes, then raffle and parking. A first-time reader knows in one sentence that this is a set of practical rules for a fete.
- The type and colour are one consistent family: one serif in bold for the headline and regular for the body, near-black on white. It reads as one calm notice, not a collage. That suits instructions, even though nothing here says "summer".

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (each kind of element looks the same everywhere; every element does a job), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No, inside the body. The headline (about 180–760 × 85–130) is clearly the first thing you see, and that part works. But the body below it has six phrases that are all underlined italic and look the same: "arrive before ten" (~258–430, y≈178), "labelled with their ingredients" (~419–734, y≈219), "three o'clock sharp" (~517–712, y≈324), "collected by four" (~180–350, y≈365) and "on the field only" (~843–960, y≈365–406). Together they cover about a third of the body text. After the headline, the eye bounces between them and finds no next step. Every rule looks equally urgent, so the one that has a real cost ("collected by four or the prizes go back in the box") gets no more weight than "parking is on the field". The underlined italics also look like links, which makes the reader wonder whether they can be clicked. That belongs to the text and interface sections, so I only note it here. Why: if everything is emphasised, nothing is. The approved source for this entry is off-list, so this is common sense and not a cited rule. To fix it, cut the emphasis down to what the reader must act on. For example, pull the times and deadlines out as a short list of lines starting with the time ("10:00 arrive", "15:00 raffle draw", "16:00 collect tickets"). Then use one plain form of emphasis, such as bold, with no underline. Taste (common sense). Weight: major. The point of the notice is for people to remember a few times and rules, and right now nothing makes them stand out.

**What's working.** The headline leads clearly: it is about twice the body size and bold, while the body is regular. That gives two levels that don't compete, which suits a notice this short. Keep that size and weight gap if you add any subheads or a list.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (one element stands clearly above the rest: six emphasised phrases of equal weight in the body).

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One shared left edge.** The heading and both paragraphs all start at x≈180 and there's only one column. Nothing is nearly aligned, so the page reads as finished and the eye never stops to check an edge.
- **The empty space is in one place.** It sits in one L-shaped area: about 300 px down the right side and roughly the bottom 45% of the frame (y≈420–800). The text stays in a single dense block, so there's a clear contrast between filled and open space, as Ruder describes in *Typography: A Manual of Design* ("Contrasts"). Because the content sits at the top, as web pages usually do, it reads as a normal short page rather than as a lopsided layout.

**Borderline calls I judged yes.** These are recorded so you can overrule them:
- **Off-centre column.** The text column is not centred: about 180 px on the left against about 300 px on the right. The gap is large enough to read as a left-set column rather than a missed centre.
- **Heading gap.** The space under the heading (≈40 px) is about the same as the space between the paragraphs. That's not a grouping problem, because the heading is the page title with nothing above it, so it can only belong to the text below.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes), Text section, 30 lines:

1 body size yes · 2 captions yes (none) · 3 upright plain face yes (only the emphasised phrases are italic) · 4 one face plan yes (one serif family) · 5 weight yes · 6 contrast yes (near-black on white) · 7 text over image yes (none) · 8 line length yes (lines run about 72 to 76 characters, at the top of the range) · 9 leading yes · 10 multi-line heading yes (none) · 11 flush left yes · 12 justified yes (none) · 13 rag yes · 14 widows/runts **no** ("only." alone on the last line, about 180,406) · 15 heading breaks yes · 16 paragraph marks yes · 17 left edge yes · 18 chunks yes · 19 mixed case yes · 20 one change for emphasis **no** (six phrases are both italic and underlined) · 21 display tighter yes · 22 kerning yes · 23 tracking yes · 24 caps spacing yes (no capital strings) · 25 ligatures yes (no fi/fl in the heading) · 26 real italics yes · 27 quotes/dashes **unsure** (apostrophe in "o'clock" at about 585,325 looks straight) · 28 tabular figures yes (none) · 29 real type yes · 30 not clipped yes.

I couldn't open the reference entries in step 5 because Bash was denied, so the deep read rests on the checklist line wording. The apostrophe stays a `no` marked "looks" until someone checks it at zoom.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each emphasized phrase change one thing only (italic, bold, or small capitals)?** No. Six phrases are set italic *and* underlined: "arrive before ten" (258–430, y≈178), "labelled with their ingredients" (419–734, y≈219), "three o'clock sharp" (517–712, y≈324), "collected by four" (180–350, y≈365), "on the field / only" (843–959 and 180–226, y≈365–406).
   - **What the viewer sees:** On a screen, italic plus underline in body text looks like a hyperlink. The reader takes these for links, tries to click them, or wonders where they go. The double emphasis also covers about a quarter of the copy, so the page looks peppered rather than stressed. Nothing stands out because almost everything does.
   - **Cost to the job:** Each phrase is a real instruction (a time, a deadline, a rule), which is exactly what should pop out. Because all six get the same treatment, the reader can't tell which one matters most.
   - **Underline problems:** The underline runs through descenders in "by", "sharp", "only" and "field", which also roughens the texture.
   - **Source:** Bringhurst; Butterick, *Practical Typography* (underline is not for emphasis in typeset text).
   - **Fix:** Pick one change. Use italic alone, or bold alone if it should scan as the key instructions, and drop the underline. Consider pulling the times and rules out into a short list so they don't need emphasis at all.
   - **Type:** Convention, and a defect here because it reads as links. **Weight:** major.
2. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** No. The second paragraph ends on "only." alone (180–232, y≈406). It also splits the emphasised phrase "on the field / only" across the break, leaving a one-word underlined stub that looks like a separate link. **Fix:** Rewrap or tie the last words with a non-breaking space so at least two words carry over. **Type:** Convention. **Weight:** minor.
3. **Are quotation marks curly, and are dashes and ellipses the true characters?** No, by eye. The apostrophe in "o'clock" (about 585,325) looks like a straight typewriter mark, not a typographer's apostrophe. **Fix:** Use ’ (U+2019), and confirm at full zoom. **Type:** Convention. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- **One serif family:** A sturdy bold serif for the heading and the matching regular for the text gives a clear two-level scale, with no competing faces.
- **Readable paragraphs:** The body is set large, near-black on white, flush left, with generous leading, and the paragraphs are split by space alone. For a short notice that people skim on a phone or a printout, this is easy to read.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Are the phrases links?** If they really are links, the underline is justified, but the italic still doubles it, and the link text doesn't say where each one goes. Check the live page.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 27 yes, 3 no (one change at a time for emphasis; widows and runts; curly quotes and true characters), 0 unsure

sections.report:
Bash is blocked, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. The image is about one screen (around 1280×800), so I judged from the whole image.

**First read.** The eye lands on the bold serif title "Notes for the summer fete", then goes to the six underlined italic phrases, which jump out of the body text. It reads as a short notice for volunteers or stallholders. It feels calm and bookish, but the underlined phrases look like links.

**Job (assumed).** A short instruction note, probably a web page or email, telling helpers the key times and rules for a village fete.

**Walk: Interface** (this section applies only because the underlined phrases look like links)
- Exactly one primary button: yes (there are no buttons)
- Controls look like what they do / links marked by more than color: **no**. Six phrases are underlined and italic at (258–430,178), (419–734,219), (517–712,324), (180–350,365), (843–960,365) and (180–226,406). Underlining is the strongest link signal on the web. These read as emphasis, not as places to go, so either the emphasis is pretending to be links or real links are dressed as emphasis.
- Non-text contrast 3:1: yes
- Hover/pressed/disabled states: yes (none shown)
- Focus indicator: unsure (can't see it in a still)
- Focus not obscured: yes
- Main content uncovered: yes
- Target size: yes for the inline-link exception. The phrases are text-height, about 20 px, and they sit inside sentences.
- Phone thumb zone: yes (not a phone layout)
- System status: yes (static notice)
- Way out: yes
- Inputs constrained: yes (no inputs)
- Destructive actions apart: yes
- Recognition over recall: yes
- Progressive disclosure: yes
- Field labels: yes
- Natural mapping: yes
- One-column form: yes
- Required markers: yes
- Errors named: yes
- Error suggestion: yes
- Empty states: yes
- Help near step: yes
- Shortcuts: yes
- Anticipation: yes
- Conventions: **no**. Underlining for emphasis breaks the web convention that underline means link (same problem as the signifier line).
- Audience's words: yes
- Link purpose from text: **no**, if these are links. "three o'clock sharp" and "on the field only" don't say where they lead.
- Sensory instructions: yes
- Conceptual model: yes
- Consistency across screens: yes
- Reflow: yes
- Honest choices: yes

---

**Section.** Interface: applies, but only just. There are no buttons, fields or navigation. The six underlined italic phrases in the body look like inline links, so the questions about links and signifiers apply.

**Findings**
1. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** (also covers *Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know*, and *Can each link's purpose be told from its text*)
   - **Where:** the six underlined italic phrases: "arrive before ten" (about x258–430, y178), "labelled with their ingredients" (x419–734, y219), "three o'clock sharp" (x517–712, y324), "collected by four" (x180–350, y365), and "on the field only" (x843–960, y365, wrapping to x180–226, y406).
   - **What the viewer meets:** on a screen, underlined text means "click here." Readers will either try to click these phrases and find nothing, or, if they are real links, have no idea where "three o'clock sharp" or "on the field only" would take them.
   - **Why:** this sends a false signal. Norman's signifiers say a mark should tell the truth about what can be done. Web convention keeps underline for links (Nielsen Norman Group; Butterick, *Practical Typography*, also says not to underline for emphasis). If they are links, their text doesn't say where they go (WCAG 2.4.4 Link purpose in context).
   - **Fix:** if they are emphasis, drop the underline and use the bold or the italic alone, not both stacked. That also cuts six emphasis marks to something quieter. If they are links, write link text that names the destination, such as "parking map" or "raffle rules", and keep the emphasis separate.
   - **Type:** defect. It misleads on any screen, and the stacked underline plus italic is taste on top of that. **Weight:** major, because these phrases carry the times and rules people will act on, and a false link signal makes readers doubt the very details they need to trust.

**What's working.** In the parts that aren't fake links, the note asks nothing of the reader: no buttons, forms or pop-ups. For a notice, the text is the whole interface, and that is right.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the underlined phrases are actually links (hover cursor, behaviour when clicked, focus ring). Check this on the live page, because it decides which of the two fixes applies.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (controls look like what they do; follow conventions; link purpose from text), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
